workPackageTitle: Immutable/double-buffered presentation snapshot and view-model primitives
notes: Entries are added before implementation and are never renumbered (docs/technical/91 § Verification registry). This file is the first commit of the W1-SIM stream: no SIM production type or test class named by a selector below exists yet.
The structural validator for this file is owned by TASK-FND-009-002. Until it lands, the shape here matches tests/verification/FND-002.json and tests/verification/FND-003.json exactly.

Status is current status: every entry is 'registered' because no implementing task has landed. A later commit flips an entry to 'implemented' only when its selector actually runs and passes, as tests/verification/FND-002.json and tests/verification/FND-003.json do.

Every nunit selector is a fully qualified 'Namespace.Class.Method' so one entry names exactly one test method. Test namespaces mirror production namespaces per doc 114 § Naming and file-placement defaults; the full type and method layout the implementation must produce is fixed in the W1-SIM design contract handed to the implementation tasks.

doc 110 registers the SIM work packages but not their task IDs. SIM-007 does not split: CTR-SIM-003 is one payload, and its immutability, versioning, double buffering, and reconstruction guarantees cannot be landed or asserted separately. Every entry belongs to TASK-SIM-007-001.

The snapshot's field list grows with every later gameplay package. This package registers the structural contract - immutability, no exposed mutable store, run and tick and version identity, double buffering, reconstruction without mutation, and the interpolation-snap policy - plus the HUD view-model rounding rule. Each later package registers its own entries for the fields it adds.

The interpolation-snap distance threshold is a derived value, not a tuning knob. Its derivation from the fastest documented authoritative movement, the tick rate, and the camera scale is recorded in the W1-SIM design contract; VER-SIM-007-007 asserts the derivation rather than a bare constant.

VER-SIM-007-009 asserts allocation-freedom as an object-identity invariant rather than a byte measurement: across many publications the double buffer cycles through exactly two PresentationSnapshot instances, never creates a third, and each page keeps the same backing storage, which is what sharing pages rather than copying untouched map state means for this design. A GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread assertion was tried first and removed: replacing any statement in SnapshotPublisher.Publish with a stub made it pass, so the residual tracked codegen of the measuring scaffold rather than the publisher, and doc 91 § Flake policy makes a flaky required test a defect. A byte-denominated per-frame allocation budget belongs to a main-tier benchmark scenario, recorded as this entry's successor QUA-005.

The note above records that SIM-007's original contract does not split. TASK-SIM-007-002 is nonetheless a real second task, on the TASK-SIM-00N-002 convention recorded in tests/verification/SIM-001.json's notes: it is the independently landable change that fenced SnapshotPublisher's staging and publication paths to the publisher's run session. It closes a gap the original contract left open rather than extending that contract, so it is its own task and its own entry.

One guard in the snapshot path is structurally unreachable from any public entry point, so nothing in this file verifies it. SnapshotDoubleBuffer.Publish refuses a publication carrying more visible entities than a page holds. Publish is internal, and its only caller, SnapshotPublisher.Publish, passes the staged span, whose length cannot exceed _stagedEntities.Length because StageVisibleEntity refuses the entity that would exceed it; both arrays are sized from the same visibleEntityCapacity constructor argument. So the staging guard fires first in every case and this one cannot fire at all. It is kept, and Publish is not made public in order to reach it, because the buffer owns its own page capacity and must not depend on its caller having checked - which is precisely what a future second caller would get wrong.

The 'platforms' list records the platforms an entry has actually been executed on, not the platforms its subject is intended to support, following tests/verification/FND-001.json and FND-002.json, which state the same convention and were corrected to it. On that reading windows-x64 and osx-arm64 are declared applicable and unexercised for every entry in this file: the subjects are portable .NET with no platform-conditional code, so they are expected to hold there, and that expectation is not coverage. linux-x64 is the only platform any run has covered. And there is no CI on this branch, so even the linux-x64 result is a local invocation on one machine rather than a runner's record; the retained artifact under artifacts/verbs/ names the invocation and its source_revision. Adding a platform back to any entry here requires a real run on it, which needs a runner FND-005 owns. No entry field holds 'applicable but unexercised': doc 91 § Verification registry lists the accepted fields and there is no 'pendingPlatforms', so this note is where the applicability claim lives rather than a field invented for it.

entries.summary: The published snapshot is immutable and exposes no mutable store: every member is read-only, no collection it returns is a store's own backing array, and no path through it reaches a mutable simulation collection.

Every snapshot carries run identity, tick, and a version that is strictly increasing across publications, so a consumer can always tell which of two snapshots is newer and whether either belongs to its run.

The snapshot is double-buffered: publishing for tick N+1 does not mutate a snapshot a consumer already holds for tick N, and the two most recent complete snapshots are simultaneously readable so presentation can interpolate between them.

A consumer can fully rebuild its presentation from one mid-run snapshot without mutating simulation state: after a complete rebuild pass the committed state, the next tick's behaviour, and the run's diagnostic checksum are bit-identical to a run in which no rebuild occurred.
A snapshot is published only in the final phase of a committed tick: no partial snapshot is ever observable, and a tick invalidated before commit publishes nothing at all rather than a partial state.

Presentation snaps rather than interpolates on spawn, teleport, boss re-entry, terminal transition, and a between-snapshot displacement above the documented distance threshold, and interpolates for every displacement below it.

The interpolation-snap distance threshold is the derived value and not a chosen constant: it is not reached by the fastest documented authoritative movement across the number of snapshot intervals the policy tolerates, and it is exceeded by the first interval beyond that, so the derivation is asserted rather than assumed.

HUD view models carry numbers that already reflect authoritative calculation and rounding: every displayed whole value equals the authoritative value after the documented rounding exactly, with no tolerance, and the view model is versioned so a consumer can detect a change without diffing fields.

Untouched static map state is not copied per tick: publishing a snapshot across a churn-free tick performs zero managed allocation after warm-up, so double buffering shares immutable pages rather than duplicating the map every tick.

A stale snapshot is droppable: a consumer that skips an arbitrary number of published snapshots still reconstructs a state consistent with the latest snapshot it did read, and never one blended from two non-adjacent snapshots.

A negative control proves the immutability and no-mutation gates can fail: a stub snapshot that hands out a store's backing array makes VER-SIM-007-001 fail, and a rebuild pass that writes through to simulation state makes VER-SIM-007-004 fail.

Staging is fenced to the publisher's run session: a snapshot entity whose identity carries a different run session is refused by StageVisibleEntity, so a reference that leaked from an earlier run cannot be published as live. The refused identity is minted by a second EntityIdAllocator on a different run session rather than by a factory, so the control exercises the only route a real caller has and collides with a live local identity on both storage index and generation.
